\chapter{Twenty, a Hundred, and the Number That Named a Family}
\label{ch:ru-round-amounts}
\hlchaptermodality{25}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say twenty and a hundred, take twenty apart into its two pieces, name which side of the centum/satem split Russian is on, and say what a Russian number still does to the noun after it that I cannot yet produce.}

The tens taken apart into numbers already known, the hundred that gives the satem branch its name, and an explicit account of the case government the numerals impose and the chapter that owes it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dvádtsat]{\ru{двадцать} — twenty, and both halves still audible}

\label{lesson:RU-C25-dvadtsat}



\begin{quote}
Count one to ten, then say ten on its own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word, and a piece}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{двадцать}} — \emph{dvádtsat} — \textbf{twenty}
\end{quote}

Take it apart and both pieces are words you have: \textbf{\ru{два}} at the front, and \textbf{-\ru{дцать}}, which is \textbf{\ru{десять}} worn down, at the back. Two tens.

That worn ending does the same job further up: \textbf{\ru{тридцать}} is three tens, thirty. Russian's tens are not a new vocabulary; they are numbers you already know with \textbf{\ru{десять}} ground down onto the end of them.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{двадцать}} — twenty
  \item \emph{Split:} \textbf{\ru{два}} + \textbf{-\ru{дцать}}
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{\ru{три}} + \textbf{-\ru{дцать}} $\to$ \textbf{\ru{тридцать}}, thirty
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D0\%B4\%D0\%B2\%D0\%B0\%D0\%B4\%D1\%86\%D0\%B0\%D1\%82\%D1\%8C}{Wiktionary: \ru{двадцать}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sto]{\ru{сто} — a hundred, and the number that named a family}

\label{lesson:RU-C25-sto}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\ru{двадцать}} and its two pieces.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ru{сто}} — \emph{sto} — \textbf{a hundred}
\end{quote}

Three letters, and the largest number this book teaches is the shortest word in it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ru{сто}} continues Indo-European *\emph{kmtom}, \textquotedblleft{}hundred.\textquotedblright{} English \textbf{hundred}, Greek \textbf{hekatón} and Latin \textbf{centum} are the same word — and \textbf{centum} is where this stops being an etymology and becomes the name of a division.

Some branches kept that first *\emph{\'{k}} as a \emph{k} sound. Latin \textbf{centum}, Greek \textbf{hekatón}, Welsh \textbf{cant} — these are the \textbf{centum} languages, named after the Latin word for a hundred.

Others turned it into an \emph{s} or an \emph{sh}. Russian \textbf{\ru{сто}}, Avestan \textbf{satəm}, Sanskrit \textbf{śatám}, Lithuanian \textbf{šimtas} — these are the \textbf{satem} languages, named after the Avestan word for the same number.

\textbf{A word for a hundred is what the two halves of the Indo-European family are named after}, and \textbf{\ru{сто}} is on the satem side. It is the same \emph{s} that survived in \textbf{\ru{шесть}} and \textbf{\ru{семь}}, doing the same work on a different consonant.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ru{сто}} — a hundred
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{\ru{сто}} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{kmtom} $\to$ Latin \textbf{centum}, English \textbf{hundred}
  \item \emph{Name:} \textbf{centum} and \textbf{satem}, and which side Russian is on
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{\ru{десять}, \ru{двадцать}, \ru{сто}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D1\%81\%D1\%82\%D0\%BE}{Wiktionary: \ru{сто}}; \href{https://www.omniglot.com/language/numbers/russian.htm}{Omniglot, Numbers in Russian}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — twelve numbers, and what they still cannot do}

\label{lesson:RU-C25-practice}



\begin{quote}
Count one to ten, then ask \textbf{\ru{сколько}}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what a Russian number does to the noun after it}]
A number in Russian does not simply sit in front of a noun. It \textbf{governs} it: \textbf{\ru{два}}, \textbf{\ru{три}} and \textbf{\ru{четыре}} take one form of the following noun and \textbf{\ru{пять}} upward takes another, and neither is the dictionary form.

This book cannot teach that yet, and saying so is more useful than skirting it. The forms it needs are the genitive singular and the genitive plural, and this track has taught the genitive in exactly one place — after \textbf{\ru{до}}, in \textbf{\ru{до} \ru{свидания}}. Counting THINGS is therefore a genitive chapter rather than a numeral one.

What the twelve numbers are already good for: answering \textbf{\ru{сколько}?} with a bare figure, giving an age, saying a price, reading a room number, and every place a number stands alone.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item Count aloud one to ten, then say \textbf{\ru{двадцать}} and \textbf{\ru{сто}}.
  \item Hear twelve amounts named singly and out of order; say each.
  \item Read the twelve printed shuffled and say each.
  \item Write all twelve from dictation.
  \item Split \textbf{\ru{двадцать}} into its two pieces and build \textbf{\ru{тридцать}} from \textbf{\ru{три}}.
  \item Say which side of the centum/satem split Russian is on, and name the number the split is named after.
\end{enumerate}
